title.narrative: Protecting Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights (PROSPECT SRHR), West Nile, Uganda

description.narrative: Goal: Improved Sexual Reproductive Health and Social Wellbeing of adolescents, young people, and women Intermediate Outcome 1: Increased access to and utilization of SRHR & SGBV services by women, adolescents and young people (10-24 years), including marginalized groups Intermediate Outcome 2: Improved retention and completion rates of girls and boys in primary and secondary schools Output Result 1: Public health facilities and community service delivery points offer integrated, quality, equitable and inclusive SRHR & SGBV services within climate and epidemic resilient health systems Output Result 2: Primary and secondary schools, and community settings have strengthened capacity to deliver sexuality education, prevent and respond to SGBV, and are safe, inclusive and adaptive to adolescent and youth needs Output Result 3: Women, adolescents and young people, especially marginalized groups, realize their SRH rights in a safe and supportive socio-cultural and policy environment at all levels Output Result 4: Women, adolescents and young people, especially marginalized groups, are economically empowered to overcome barriers to access and utilization of SRHR, SGBV & education services Output Result 5: Governance and accountability mechanisms for social services (Health, Education, SGBV Response) are strengthened at all levels within the district social services delivery system

Primary targeted beneficiary groups under the project: • Adolescents and young people aged 10-24 (including those not in education, employment, or training (NEETS), people living with disabilities (PWDs), and teenage mothers) AND women of a reproductive age of 25-49 years. • A sub-set of the primary beneficiary groups above are multi-dimensional marginalized groups e.g. refugees, those living in extreme poverty and hard-to-reach communities, child headed households Secondary beneficiaries include: • Men, community leaders, political, religious and cultural leaders, and community groups; • District local governments and lower local (sub county and parish) governments, particularly staff in Health, Education and Community Development departments

The Protecting Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights (PROSPECT SRHR) project in West Nile, Uganda is a 4-year initiative funded by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and implemented by the International Rescue Committee (IRC) in consortium with World Vision Uganda (WVU), Reach A Hand Uganda (RAHU), Humanity and Inclusion (HI), with Open Capital Advisors (OCA) as a strategic technical partner. It seeks to improve the sexual and reproductive health and social wellbeing of adolescents, young people and women of reproductive age by contributing to reductions in preventable maternal deaths, teenage pregnancies, sexual and gender-based violence, child marriage and new HIV infections. The Activity operates in Yumbe, Koboko, Maracha, Terego, Nebbi and Pakwach districts. It prioritizes adolescents and young people aged 10-24 years, women of reproductive age, teenage mothers, young people not in education, employment or training, refugees, persons with disabilities and people living in hard-to-reach communities. It also engages men, parents, caregivers, community leaders, religious and cultural leaders, schools, health facilities, district local governments and community structures that influence access to health, education, protection and social services. The Activity responds to persistent barriers that affect access to quality sexual and reproductive health, protection and education services in West Nile. These include weak adolescent responsive and inclusive service delivery, gaps in health worker capacity, commodity stock outs, weak referral systems, harmful gender and social norms, school dropout linked to pregnancy and poverty, limited support for teenage mothers to return to school, stigma faced by young people and persons with disabilities, weak data systems and limited accountability in service delivery. The intervention uses an integrated systems strengthening approach that connects health facilities, schools and communities. It strengthens public health facilities and community service delivery points to provide quality, equitable, inclusive and youth friendly SRHR and SGBV services within climate and epidemic resilient health systems. This includes mentorship and capacity building for health workers, community health workers, peer providers and village health teams; improved provision of family planning, maternal health, post abortion care, postpartum family planning, clinical management of rape, adolescent health, HIV and STI related services; and support for quality of care improvement. PROSPECT SRHR strengthens reproductive health commodity security through improved ordering, stock monitoring, supply chain review, digital tools and district led corrective action. The Activity supports schools and community settings to deliver age-appropriate sexuality education, prevent and respond to SGBV, and promote safe and inclusive learning environments. It works with teachers, school leadership structures, parent groups, learners, community actors and district education teams to strengthen life skills education, menstrual health, school clubs, referral pathways, disability inclusion, learner tracking and support for the re-entry of teenage mothers into school. The Activity works with women, adolescents and young people to increase agency, participation and demand for services. Through peer educators, youth champions, Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSS), community dialogues, intergenerational engagement, mass media, digital media and youth led platforms, the Activity promotes informed decision making and addresses social norms that limit access to SRHR, SGBV and education services. It also engages political, religious, cultural and community leaders to support positive attitudes toward adolescent health, prevention of violence, disability inclusion, school retention and the rights of teenage mothers. The Activity addresses economic barriers that limit access to services and increase vulnerability to early marriage, teenage pregnancy, school dropout, exploitation and violence. It supports financial literacy, savings groups, vocational and entrepreneurship skills, business mentorship, market linkages and livelihood pathways for vulnerable young people and women. The Activity also strengthens governance, accountability, planning, data use and sustainable financing for health, education and protection services. It supports district local governments, schools, health facilities and community structures to improve coordination, joint planning, performance monitoring, data quality, routine data use and participatory accountability. It promotes community feedback mechanisms, client satisfaction processes, community scorecards, citizen voice and action approaches, joint monitoring, data quality assessments, performance review meetings and use of routine information systems such as HMIS, DHIS2, EMIS, iHRIS and GBV information systems. It also supports disability inclusion in planning, budgeting, implementation and monitoring, while exploring innovative financing approaches for sustainable SRHR and SGBV service delivery. Across all components, the Activity applies human rights, gender equality, disability inclusion, meaningful youth participation, safeguarding, accountability to affected populations, social inclusion and evidence-based programming. It works through existing government systems and district structures, aligns with national policies and guidelines, and promotes local ownership. The overall approach is designed to strengthen systems, improve service quality, increase use of services, support school retention and completion, reduce protection risks and improve the wellbeing of adolescents, young people and women in West Nile, Uganda.

title.narrative: OP5.11 Number of communities, CSOs and advocacy networks with increased lobby & advocacy capacities

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of Community-Led Monitors (CLMs) or Citizen Voice and Action (CVA), drawn from selected community resource persons, whose capacity to engage in lobby and advocacy for SRHR, SGBV, and education service improvements has demonstrably increased during the reporting period. CLMs operate at subcounty and parish level, representing empowered community structures responsible for monitoring service delivery, documenting issues, and engaging duty bearers.

title.narrative: OP5.10 Number of youth who participate in policy and decision making bodies who perceive their participation as meaningful

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of young people aged 10 to 24 years who are formally represented in recognized policy, planning, governance, accountability, or decision-making bodies, and who report that their participation was meaningful during the reporting period. A youth should be counted only when all THREE conditions are met: 1. The youth participated in a recognized decision-making body, such as a district or sub county planning forum, District Technical Planning Committee, youth council, school governance structure, Health Unit Management Committee, community accountability platform, District Child and Adolescent Health Committee, OPD platform, or other formal governance structure. 2. The participation is verified through at least one official record, such as meeting minutes, attendance list, membership list, action tracker, appointment letter, nomination record, or platform report. 3. The youth reports that their participation was meaningful, based on a short perception tool, feedback form, interview, or reflection session. Meaningful participation means that the youth was given space to speak, was listened to, contributed to discussion, raised an issue, influenced a decision, shaped an action point, or received feedback on issues raised.

title.narrative: OP5.7 Number of actions agreed from accountability dialogues, that were implemented by district, subcounty and community leadership (health facility, schools & community) to remove barriers to utilization of services and strengthen SRHR for all.

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of actions agreed upon during accountability dialogues that were implemented by district, subcounty, and community leadership (including health facilities, schools, and community leaders) to remove barriers to the utilization of services and strengthen Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) for all individuals. Actions are counted only if they are formally agreed upon in accountability dialogues and subsequently implemented, as verified through follow-up monitoring.

title.narrative: OP5.6 Number of accountability dialogues held at district, subcounty and community level including schools on social service delivery and SRHR for all and address SGBV

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of evidence-based and accountability dialogues held at the district, subcounty, and community levels, and schools focusing on social service delivery, SRHR for all, and addressing SGBV. These dialogues are structured discussions aimed at promoting community engagement, raising awareness, and holding relevant stakeholders accountable for improving service delivery related to SRHR and addressing SGBV. This could include among others annual dialogue between health providers and people, parents and teachers, teachers-learners, barazas between subcounty officials and the people, at district level you can have between district leaders and people.

title.narrative: OP5.3 Number of districts with functional Maternal and Perinatal Death Review and Response (MPDSR)committees

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of districts that have established and maintain functional Maternal and Perinatal Death Review and Response (MPDR) committees to systematically review maternal and perinatal deaths and implement response actions to improve maternal and newborn health outcomes. A district is counted if it has an active MPDR committee that meets the national guidelines, conducts regular reviews, and implements response actions. Functionality is assessed through meeting minutes, reports, implementation of recommendations, and stakeholder verification.

title.narrative: OP5.2 Number of districts with functional District Committee on Adolescent Health (DICAH)

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of districts with a functional District Committee on Adolescent Health (DICAH), ensuring coordinated efforts to address adolescent health needs, including Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) and Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV). It is a multi-sectoral district-level body responsible for planning, coordinating, and monitoring adolescent health interventions. It typically includes representatives from the district health office, education department, community development, civil society organizations, and youth representatives. A DICAH is considered functional if it meets regularly (as per established guidelines), has documented minutes/action points, actively oversees adolescent health programs, and engages in policy implementation or advocacy.

title.narrative: OP5.4 Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) reviews reported

description.narrative: Percentage of facility-level MDSR review reports documented in the Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance Summary reports. Ending preventable maternal and perinatal mortality is an essential ingredient of the Sustainable Development Goals. Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response reviews are an important step in identifying the underlying causes and formulating the relevant quality improvement plans

title.narrative: OP5.1 Number of districts/or sub-counties with functional and effective government led coordination mechanisms on SRHR, SGBV and Education issues

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of districts or sub-counties that have functional and effective government-led coordination mechanisms focused on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR), Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV), and Education. Functional and effective coordination mechanism: Refers to the existence of a structured, active platform where relevant government entities, stakeholders, and service providers collaboratively plan, coordinate, and monitor actions, policies, and programs related to SRHR, SGBV, and education. The mechanism should demonstrate clear roles, responsibilities, regular communication, meet routinely and coordination across sectors and institutions.
Improved Sexual Reproductive Health and Social Wellbeing of adolescents, young people, and women

title.narrative: Number of new HIV infections among adolescents and young people

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of new HIV infections reported among adolescents and young people (aged 10-24 years) within the reporting period. It tracks the incidence of HIV infections in this age group to assess the effectiveness of interventions aimed at HIV prevention, education, and service delivery targeted at adolescents and young people.
Increased access to and utilization of SRHR & SGBV services by women, adolescents and young people (10-24), including marginalized groups

title.narrative: OC1.1b Number of women and girls using modern contraceptives (Revisits)

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of women and girls who return for continued use of a modern contraceptive method within the reporting period at any health facility, outreach, or community delivery point. It captures continuing clients, who have already initiated a modern method in the past and now present for: - method resupply - reinjection - follow-up - removal and reinsertion (for LARCs) - counseling related to continued use Rationale: This indicator reflects method continuation, service utilization patterns, and contraceptive adherence which is key to sustaining modern contraceptive coverage and preventing unintended pregnancies.

title.narrative: OC1.4 Decreased Institutional Maternal Mortality Ratio in health facilities in targeted districts

description.narrative: The Institutional maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is used to measure maternal mortality within health facilities, specifically the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births occurring in those facilities. It's a key metric for assessing the quality and effectiveness of maternal healthcare services provided in hospitals and other healthcare institutions. Maternal deaths: The annual number of female deaths from any cause related to or aggravated by pregnancy or its management (excluding accidental or incidental causes) during pregnancy and childbirth or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, expressed per 100,000 live births, for a specified time period.

title.narrative: OC1.1a Number of women and girls using modern contraceptives (New Users)

description.narrative:
This indicator measures the number of women and girls who are currently using modern contraceptive methods within the reporting period. It reflects the uptake of modern contraception as an essential component of reproductive health services and family planning programs. A new user is that one who: a) Has never used a modern contraceptive method before, and starts using one during the reporting period, OR b) Previously used a modern method but discontinued and remained non-users for at least 3 months, and restart a method during the reporting period, OR c) Is postpartum/post-abortion case and adopts a modern method during this period for the first time or after prolonged non-use, OR d) Switches from traditional to modern methods for the first time in the reporting period.
Modern contraceptive methods include: Oral Pills, IUDs, Implants, Injectables-Intramuscular, Injectables-Subcutaneous, Condoms (Male & Female), Sterilization, Fertility Awareness Methods, Emergency Contraceptives etc.
Rationale: Tracking new users helps programs to measure expansion of contraceptive access, detect increases in demand generation effectiveness, identify gaps among adolescents and underserved groups, support resource planning for FP commodity security, align with Uganda’s FP2030 commitments and annual reporting

title.narrative: OC1.5 Proportion of births attended by skilled health personnel in target districts

description.narrative: Percent of births attended by skilled health personnel (doctors, nurses or midwives) trained in providing life-saving obstetric care, including giving the necessary supervision, care and advice to women during pregnancy, childbirth and the postpartum period, and for their newborns

title.narrative: OC1.3 Improved Couple Years of Protection

description.narrative: The estimated protection provided by family planning services during a one-year period, based upon the volume of all contraceptives sold or distributed free of charge to clients during that period. CYP helps measure the reach and impact of family planning programs. Calculation: The CYP is calculated by multiplying the quantity of each method distributed to clients by a conversion factor, which yields an estimate of the duration of contraceptive protection provided per unit of that method.

Primary and secondary schools, and community settings have strengthened capacity to deliver sexuality education, prevent and respond to SGBV, and are safe, inclusive and adaptive to adolescent and youth needs

title.narrative: OP2.2 Number of resource persons with capacity built to provide age appropriate SRHR/SGBV information to young people

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of resource persons in school settings who have had their capacity built during the reporting period to deliver age-appropriate information on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) to young people aged 10–24 years. Resource persons: include senior women and men, school management team members, counseling and guidance teachers, school club patrons, class teachers etc. Age-appropriate information: Content tailored to the developmental stage of the target audience, covering topics such as puberty, consent, contraception, HIV/STIs, healthy relationships, and GBV prevention. Capacity building: Refers to participation in structured training, mentorship, or coaching sessions and provision of job aids that equip individuals with the knowledge, skills, and tools to effectively facilitate SRHR/SGBV education in schools settings.

title.narrative: OP2.4 Number of teenage mothers (10-19years) reintegrated back to school

description.narrative: This indicator measures the proportion of young people aged 10–24 years who demonstrate comprehensive and correct knowledge about HIV prevention, transmission, treatment and misconceptions. It reflects the effectiveness of HIV education efforts in equipping youth with the knowledge needed to protect themselves and others. Comprehensive and correct knowledge of HIV includes the ability to: 1) Identify primary ways of preventing sexual transmission of HIV (e.g., consistent condom use and being faithful to one uninfected partner) 2) Reject common misconceptions about HIV transmission (e.g., HIV can be transmitted by mosquito bites or sharing food) 3) Know that a healthy looking person can have HIV 4) Rejecting the common local misconceptions that HIV can be transmitted through mosquito bites or supernatural means 5) Rejecting the common local misconceptions that HIV can be transmitted through shring food with a person who has HIV or AIDS A respondent must answer all five components correctly to be counted as having comprehensive and correct knowledge.

title.narrative: OP2.1 Number of primary and secondary schools strengthened to provide age-appropriate SRHR/SGBV information to young people
OP2.9 Number of girls in targeted schools provided with safe and quality reusable menstrual pads

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of female learners in targeted primary and secondary schools who receive safe, quality, and reusable menstrual pads provided through the PROTECT SRHR project aimed at improving school attendance, dignity, and participation, while reducing absenteeism due to menstruation. Rationale: Absence of supportive MHM practices is a critical barrier to adolescent girls’ education and wellbeing as it leads to absenteeism during menstruation due to lack of sanitary products, inadequate school WASH facilities, or stigma.
Public health facilities and community service delivery points offer integrated, quality, equitable and inclusive SRHR & SGBV services within climate and epidemic resilient health systems

title.narrative: OP1.16 Number of individuals provided with comprehensive Post Abortion Care (PAC) services

description.narrative: The indicator counts unique individuals (women, adolescents, and others of reproductive age) who received comprehensive Post-Abortion Care (PAC) at a health facility or through an outreach/mobile team during the reporting period. Comprehensive PAC means the person received the full PAC package as defined by WHO (2022) and Ugandan clinical guidance: - emergency treatment of abortion complications (including stabilization and treatment of bleeding, sepsis, uterine evacuation where needed) - counseling (including for emotional needs and danger signs) - provision of voluntary family-planning counseling and method(s) of their choice before discharge (including emergency contraception if appropriate) - STI/HIV screening/linkage as appropriate and - referral/continuity of care services (e.g., follow-up, psychosocial support, legal or social services where relevant). A client is counted once in the reporting period even if they return for follow-up (de-duplicate by unique client ID, file number, or combined identifiers).

title.narrative: OP1.19 Number of maternal deaths averted.

description.narrative: This captures the estimated number of maternal deaths averted due to project support. Maternal death is the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.

title.narrative: OP1.14 Number of young people reached with comprehensive, correct information on sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy, and contraception and GBV prevention and response.

description.narrative: This indicator assesses the total number of individuals aged 10–24 years who are engaged through program activities that provide thorough and accurate information on: i) Sexuality (such as puberty, consent, and healthy relationships) ii) HIV/AIDS and STIs (including transmission, prevention, testing, and treatment) iii) Pregnancy and Contraception (covering causes, prevention methods, as well as myths and facts) iv) Gender-Based Violence (GBV) (encompassing types, prevention strategies, response measures, rights, and services) The information must be conveyed through structured, age appropriate channels like school clubs, peer education sessions, community dialogues, digital platforms (i.e. Social media campaigns, Linkedin, SMS surveys, cinemas, recorded games and dramas etc), or health outreach initiatives.

title.narrative: OP1.18 Number of unsafe abortions averted

description.narrative: This indicator estimates the number of unsafe abortions that were prevented due to access to modern contraceptive methods, and post-abortion care. It reflects the impact of reproductive health interventions in reducing the incidence of unsafe abortion practices. Unsafe abortions are a significant public health issue, often resulting from unintended pregnancies and lack of access to safe abortion services. Preventing unsafe abortions through improved access to contraception and safe reproductive health services is essential for safeguarding women's health and rights. This will be modelled in MSI’s Impact 2.5 tool from routine service statistics.

title.narrative: OP1.17 Number of unintended pregnancies averted

description.narrative: This indicator measures the estimated number of pregnancies that were prevented during a specified reference period due to the use of modern contraceptive methods, family planning services, or reproductive health interventions. Unintended pregnancies can have significant health, social, and economic consequences for individuals and communities. Preventing them through access to effective contraception and reproductive health services is an important public health goal. This indicator provides a quantifiable measure of progress toward that goal. Rationale: The indicator assumes that all couples currently using contraception want to avoid a pregnancy and that if they did not have access to modern contraception they would be at risk of an unintended pregnancy. Unintended pregnancies that result due to method failure are subtracted from this calculation - so in places where more effective contraceptive methods are used, a relatively larger number of pregnancies will be averted.

title.narrative: Op1.7 Number of health facilities implementing climate smart and epidemic resilient SRHR service delivery models

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of health facilities that have adopted and are actively implementing climate smart and epidemic resilient strategies in SRHR service delivery. These strategies may include, stockpiling essential SRHR supplies, telehealth services, CMEs, solar powered facilities to overcome power outages during severe weather, IEC materials on climate and health, multisectoral collaboration, and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures etc. Rationale: Climate change and disease outbreaks pose significant threats to SRHR service continuity. Facilities that integrate climate resilience and epidemic preparedness can better sustain essential services, reducing service disruptions and improving health outcomes.

title.narrative: OP1.1 Number of service providers (health workers and community health workers) trained/mentored on integrated, quality, equitable, and inclusive SRHR & SGBV services

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of health workers and community health workers who complete at least one structured training or mentorship session on integrated, quality, equitable, and inclusive SRHR and SGBV services within the reporting period.

title.narrative: OP1.10 Number of adolescents and young people, and women of a reproductive age that received STI management (including HIV counselling and testing).

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of adolescents, young people, and women of reproductive age who receive Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI) management services within a given reporting period. STI management refers to any clinical, preventive, diagnostic, counselling, or treatment service provided for sexually transmitted infections, including HIV counselling and HIV testing.

title.narrative: OP1.9 Number of adolescents and young people, and women of a reproductive age provided with SRHR services (ANC1, Safe Delivery, Postpartum, Cervical Cancer Screening and Management, HP Vaccination).

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of unique adolescents, young people and women of reproductive age who receive any of the following core Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) services within the reporting period (ANC1, safe delivery - skilled birth attendance, postpartum care, cervical cancer screening, HPV vaccination. This indicator captures coverage, reach, and performance of the SRHR continuum of care from pregnancy through childbirth, postpartum, cancer prevention, and adolescent SRH services. It is essential for: - Reducing maternal morbidity and mortality - Improving adolescent SRHR outcomes - Ensuring continuity of care for mothers - Addressing cervical cancer burden - Increasing uptake of HPV vaccination - Supporting Uganda’s RMNCAH priorities and global commitments

title.narrative: OP1.8 Number of health workers trained on climate change adaptation, disaster preparedness, and epidemic response for SRHR service continuity

description.narrative: This indicator tracks the number of health workers who have completed formal training on climate change adaptation, emergency preparedness, and epidemic response strategies in the context of SRHR service delivery. Rationale: Trained health workers are essential for maintaining SRHR service provision during climate crises and epidemics. Capacity-building efforts improve their ability to implement adaptive strategies, ensuring service continuity for vulnerable populations.

title.narrative: OP1.13 Number of individuals (including young people), reached with SRHR/SGBV information/sensitization and mobilization to transform social norms who demonstrate improved attitudes and practices towards the elimination of all forms of violence, including harmful practices .

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of individuals (adolescents, youth, women, men, community and religious leaders, and other stakeholders) who have been reached through social and behavior change (SBC) interventions under the PROTECT SRHR project and who demonstrate measurable positive change in their attitudes and/or practices related to sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) and harmful practices (such as child marriage, female genital mutilation/cutting, or intimate partner violence).

title.narrative: OP1.12 Number of individuals (including young people), reached with SRHR/SGBV information/sensitization and mobilization to transform social norms
OP1.11 Number of adolescents and young people, and women of a reproductive age that experienced SGBV and accessed post-SGBV health services (including mental health).

description.narrative: Measures the total number of individuals who have received services in response to SGBV. Service type categories include: Health: Medical treatment and healthcare services provided to SGBV survivors, including emergency medical care sexual and reproductive health services(PEP, ECP), and HIV/AIDS-related testing and counselling. Psychosocial: Mental health and psychosocial support services, including, support groups, and specialized psychological therapy. Economic: Economic empowerment services, such as referrals for vocational training (formal and non-Formal), and livelihood support programs.

title.narrative: OP1.6 Percentage of targeted CEmONC & BEmONC facilities meeting the minimum standards for availability, usability and quality of signal functions for emergency obstetric and newborn care

description.narrative: This indicator measures the percentage of beneficiaries who report being satisfied with the quality of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV), and HIV/AIDS services they received. Satisfaction is assessed based on key service quality dimensions such as respectful care, confidentiality, timeliness, availability of services, provider competence etc.

title.narrative: OP1.5 Percentage of beneficiaries satisfied with quality of SRHR & SGBV & HIV/AIDS services.

description.narrative:
This indicator measures the percentage of beneficiaries who report being satisfied with the quality of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV), and HIV/AIDS services they received.
Satisfaction is assessed based on key service quality dimensions such as respectful care, confidentiality, timeliness, availability of services, provider competence etc.

title.narrative: OP1.4 Number of health facilities providing youth-friendly SRHR & SGBV & HIV/AIDS services

description.narrative: This indicator counts the number of health facilities that offer youth friendly SRHR, SGBV, and HIV/AIDS services, ensuring accessibility, acceptability, and appropriateness for young people. Youth friendly services: Services that are accessible, acceptable, equitable, appropriate, and effective for adolescents and young people e.g. - Confidentiality and ensuring audio and visual privacy - Contraceptive services - STI and HIV testing and treatment - SGBV clinical management and referral - SRHR education and information - Respectful, non-discriminatory care by trained providers

title.narrative: OP1.2 Percent of relevant health workers in health facilities supported by the project that meet competency Level 1 in the services they provide

description.narrative: This indicators measures the number of healthcare workers who have been trained/mentored and have achieved Level 1 competence demonstrated by their ability to provide quality services. Level 1 means the provider is competent to provide FP (e.g. implant, IUD) or PAC (e.g. medical abortion or manual vacuum aspiration) services unsupervised depending on the services being supported at each facility Level 2 requires supervision; and Level 3 means the provider is unable to provide the service until further training has been completed.

title.narrative: OP1.3 Percent of health facilities experiencing no stock-outs of at least three modern FP methods over a period of three consecutive months

description.narrative: This indicator measures the percentage of health facilities that maintain continuous availability of at least three modern family planning (FP) methods without stock-outs for three consecutive months within the reporting period.
Women, adolescents and young people, especially marginalized groups, are economically empowered to overcome barriers to access and utilization of SRHR, SGBV & education services

title.narrative: OP4.1 Percentage of program participants whose monthly personal income increased from IGAs, VSILAs, or business activities by the end of the program period.

description.narrative: This indicator measures the percentage of program participants who show an increase in income by the end of the program period, as evidenced by self-reported income improvements supplemented with verifiable sources such as savings records, business financial logs, or VSILA contributions. It assesses whether project interventions have contributed to economic empowerment through employment, business activities, or income generating initiatives.
Women, adolescents and young people, especially marginalized groups, realize their SRH rights in a safe and supportive socio-cultural and policy environment at all levels

title.narrative: OP3.7 Number of religious and cultural institutions that develop and effectively implement action plans to shift negative gender and social norms affecting demand and utilization of SRHR & SGBV services among women and adolescent girls.

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of religious and cultural institutions that develop and effectively implement action plans aimed at shifting negative gender and social norms that hinder the demand for and utilization of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) and Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV) services among women and adolescent girls. A growing number of institutions implementing such plans indicates increasing institutional ownership and leadership in transforming harmful norms. It also reflects progress toward sustainable, community-led change in gender and health outcomes.

title.narrative: OP3.4 Number of community resource persons trained/mentored to provide age appropriate SRHR/SGBV information to young people

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of community based individuals who receive structured training and/or mentorship from the PROTECT SRHR project to deliver accurate, age-appropriate, and evidence based SRHR and SGBV information to adolescents and young people. It captures both training and mentorship sessions that enable these resource persons to competently support young people with SRHR/SGBV information, referrals, and risk reduction messages. Community resource persons include: VHTs, EMAP Allies, SASA activists, peer educators, parasocial workers, community based volunteers, community linkage facilitators.

title.narrative: OP3.1 Number of adolescents and young people, and women of reproductive age, including marginalized groups, reached by life skills programs (e.g. Girl Shine [for In-School and Out-of-School], WGSS, School clubs, Livelihood groups) that build their health and social assets

description.narrative: This indicator tracks the number of adolescents, young people (10-24 years), and women of reproductive age (25-49 years) who actively participate in structured life skills programs e.g. (Girl Shine, WGSS, School clubs, livelihood groups) designed to enhance their health and social assets. The PROTECT SRHR project recognizes that economic and social barriers often limit women and young people’s ability to access and utilize SRHR services. By building their health, financial, and social assets, these programs empower them to make informed decisions about their reproductive health, education, and economic opportunities​. Reached: Refers to individuals who have actively participated in life skills sessions and have completed at least 75% of the sessions or core training module. Health and Social Assets: Refers to the knowledge, skills, attitudes, and social networks that empower individuals to make healthy life choices, including understanding SRHR, negotiating healthy relationships, and resisting harmful social norms.

title.narrative: OP3.5 Number of cultural and religious leaders reached with information on elimination of all forms of violence including harmful practice and promoting gender equality practices

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of cultural and religious leaders who have been engaged through training, sensitization sessions, meetings, dialogues, or outreach activities aimed at increasing their awareness and capacity to advocate for the elimination of all forms of violence including harmful traditional practices and to promote gender equality within their communities. A higher number indicates increased outreach and potential influence on community norms through key opinion leaders. However, follow-up assessments are needed to evaluate changes in attitudes and practices resulting from the engagement.

title.narrative: OP3.2 Number of SGBV survivors referred by the program to access justice services

description.narrative: This indicator counts the number of SGBV survivors referred by the program to access justice services, including legal aid, law enforcement, or court processes, within the reporting period. A higher number indicates improved survivor access to justice and stronger referral systems. However, it should be interpreted alongside data on case outcomes, survivor satisfaction, and barriers to justice to assess the quality and impact of referrals. SGBV survivor: Is an individual who has experienced violence, coercion, or other harmful acts based on their gender. It includes various forms of violence, such as sexual assault, domestic violence, forced marriage, and emotional abuse, all of which are rooted in gender inequality.
